You can use various tenses in your writing to relate events or tell stories.

You can write in narrative tenses when you want to tell a story or recall past events. The tenses are the Simple Past, Past Continuous and Past Perfect. You can use these tenses in the affirmative, negative and interrogative form (questions).
Remember not to mix present and past tenses when you are narrating.
Sojourner Truth, a self-given name, was born into slavery in 1797.
She and her family were living on an estate, 95 miles north of New York until 1806.
In 1700, the state of New York was beginning to negotiate the abolition of slavery.
During the Civil War, Truth helped recruit black troops for the Union Army.
Soon after, she petitioned the court to secure the release of one of her children who had been taken to the South.

images.text: Sojourner Truth, a self-given name,  was born into slavery  in 1797. Her father, James Baumfree was a slave captured in modern-day Ghana and her mother Mau-Mau Bet, was the daughter of slaves from Guinea. She and her family were living on an estate, 95 miles north of New York until 1806. At 9, Truth was sold at an auction with a flock of sheep for $100. She was passed off to a number of harsh and violent slave owners, finally coming to reside on a property at West Park, New York.

It was during this period that Truth learned to speak English. In 1700, the state of New York was beginning to negotiate the abolition of slavery. They emancipated all slaves in 1827. Soon after, she petitioned the court to secure the release of one of her children who had been taken to the South.  Her case was one of the first in which a black woman successfully challenged a white man in a United States court. In 1843, Truth changed her name from Isabella Baumfree and devoted her life to the Methodist church and the abolition of slavery. Furthermore, she joined the Northampton Association of Education and Industry, a group fighting for women's rights and pacifism.

During the Civil War, Truth helped recruit black troops  for the Union Army. On several occasions, she met with President Abraham Lincoln to discuss her beliefs and experiences. Sojourner Truth died on November 26th, 1883 and is buried alongside her family at Battle Creek. This determined and courageous woman continued to speak passionately on women's rights, prison reform and universal suffrage till the end of her life.
